clue.text: No college boy's beaten an average player

indicators.note: beaten as in battered out of shape, so the letters of these words are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A sporting rebuke: someone who never went to college has been beaten by a mediocre performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten' reworks the twelve letters of NO COLLEGE BOY; the 's is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf the imaginary opponent who scores the bogey (par-level) total on every hole was called by this name, so he plays to an average standard.

clue.text: Following orders, excellent to get up during illness

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means rising, so the excellent pair inside the illness word is turned upside down where it sits

parts.note: a complaint is an ailment or illness
A1 means first-rate, written AI

explanation.surface: A soldier who obeys orders even though they have to rise from a sickbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The A and I already sit in the middle of COMPLAINT; 'to get up during' flips them in place to IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone compliant obeys and goes along with what they are told, an adjectival synonym.

clue.text: Red Square is up: being old fashioned, want to go round

indicators.note: going round means the archaic word surrounds the turned number

parts.note: list is an archaic verb meaning to wish or want

indicators.note: in a down clue being up means the number word is written bottom to top

parts.note: nine is a square number, three times three

explanation.surface: A Moscow scene: Red Square is built up, and an old-fashioned longing surrounds it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Square' looks like the Moscow landmark, but Red is the definition and the square is a number. 'is up' turns it over and 'to go round' wraps the archaic verb about it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Red is a communist, and a follower of the Bolshevik leader's doctrine is one such communist.

clue.text: Cold, like a crab's claws?

definitions.meaning: pincers that nip, read playfully as given to nipping

explanation.surface: A seaside query about chilly weather and the bite of a crab.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a playful coinage, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Chilly weather is called nippy, and claws that pinch could jokingly be described the same way.

clue.text: Large furniture maker knocks up large quantities, probably

parts.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
IKEA is the Swedish flat-pack furniture company

indicators.note: in a down clue knocking up means pushing upward, so the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: tons means lots

explanation.surface: A big flat-pack retailer churns out huge volumes of stock, most likely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocks up' turns TONS into SNOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means more likely than not, so it is an idiom for probably.

clue.text: Inspection team ejected with force, not united

indicators.note: with one letter and not another means the force letter is put where the united letter was
with one letter and not another means the force letter is put where the united letter was

parts.note: ousted means thrown out
U is the abbreviation for United in team names
F is the physics symbol for force

explanation.surface: Inspectors are thrown out forcibly, no longer acting together.
explanation.walkthrough: OFSTED is the UK government body that inspects schools.
explanation.definitionFit: The Office for Standards in Education sends out inspectors to assess English schools.

clue.text: Former officer receives half an honour

indicators.note: receiving means the officer takes something in

parts.note: ex means former
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

indicators.note: half of a two-letter word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A retired officer is given part of a decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes A from 'an'; it goes inside EXLT.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt someone is to raise them high in esteem, a verb synonym of honour.

clue.text: Set about a journey by sea, say

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken rather than written

parts.note: a sail is a trip in a boat, so the phrase is 'a sail'

explanation.surface: Starting out on a voyage, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set about' looks like 'begin'; here it means attack. 'say' tells you to voice 'a sail'.
explanation.definitionFit: To set about someone is to attack them, and to assail is to attack.

clue.text: Shreds chapter to be used in extracts

indicators.note: being used in means the chapter letter goes inside the other word

parts.note: mines means digs out or extracts

explanation.surface: An editor tears up a chapter to use parts of it in excerpts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extracts' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To mince food is to chop it finely, so it shreds it.

clue.text: Chap working at a sort of card

indicators.note: at puts the working word next to the card word

parts.note: a SIM card goes in a mobile phone
on means operating or working

explanation.surface: A man busy with some kind of card.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon is a man's name, and crosswords use any male name for chap.

clue.text: Coffin covered in betel leaf, one for a Muslim, probably

indicators.note: being covered in means the coffin word is wrapped inside the leaf word

parts.note: paan is the betel-leaf preparation chewed across South Asia
kist is a Scots word for a chest or coffin
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A coffin wrapped in betel leaf, offered to a probable Muslim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'probably' because most, not all, Pakistanis are Muslims.
explanation.definitionFit: Pakistan is an overwhelmingly Islamic country, so a citizen is likely to be a follower of Islam.

clue.text: More than enough to convert penalty

indicators.note: converting means turning one form into another, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rugby or football side has more than enough chances to score from a spot kick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'convert' plays on scoring a penalty but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word means in abundance, which is more than enough.

clue.text: Shaking off cold, one doubting being free of germs

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: shaking off means getting rid of, so the cold letter is removed

parts.note: sceptic as an adjective means doubting
C is the tap abbreviation for cold

explanation.surface: Getting over a cold, a doubter finds himself germ-free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shaking off' removes the first C of SCEPTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means sterile, with no harmful bacteria present.

clue.text: Clock change in spring getting support

parts.note: a leap is a jump or spring
to second a motion is to support it

explanation.surface: The clocks go forward in spring, with general backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' suggests the season, but means a jump.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra second is occasionally added to official clock time, a one-second adjustment.

clue.text: Came and collected what is necessary

definitions.meaning: someone who calls to pick something up has fetched it
a situation that demands something requires it

explanation.surface: A courier picked up what was needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Collecting a parcel is fetching it in person; a remark that was needed was demanded by the situation.

clue.text: Flower girl's brief stand

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the name loses its final letter

parts.note: Daisy is a girl's name that is also a flower

explanation.surface: A girl who carries flowers at a wedding gets a short moment on the stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower girl' looks like the bridesmaid but is a girl named after a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais is a raised platform for speakers, a kind of stand.

clue.text: Badly translated old manual so eccentric

indicators.note: a bad translation mangles the text, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A poorly translated old instruction book makes no sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Anomalous means irregular or odd, so it is a synonym of eccentric.

clue.text: What gets insect drunk, like sheep, perhaps?

parts.note: what makes someone drunk is a drink such as rum
in means gets in, the drink going into the creature
an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what would make an insect tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'What gets insect drunk' as RUM IN ANT: rum put into an ant.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep chew the cud, and animals that do so are classed by this adjective; 'perhaps' because cattle are too.

clue.text: The American behind strike

explanation.surface: An American's rear end delivers a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call the buttocks this, and goats or rams hit with their heads in a matching verb.

clue.text: From this doctor's manner, only one died nearby

indicators.note: only one means the word keeps just one of its two died letters

parts.note: a doctor's way with patients is the bedside manner

explanation.surface: A doctor's manner was so poor that just one patient died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only one' drops one of the two Ds from BEDSIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Beside means next to, so close at hand.

clue.text: Judge put our lad off recommended course

indicators.note: off means gone bad or awry, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A judge puts a young man off a course recommended to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' means a dish in a meal; 'off' mixes J with PUTOURLAD.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means dish of the day, a menu course the restaurant is recommending.

clue.text: Native Australian had meal under cover

parts.note: a roo is a kangaroo, native to Australia
fed means ate or had a meal

explanation.surface: An Aboriginal Australian ate indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native Australian' suggests a person, but is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something roofed has a roof over it, so it is covered.

clue.text: Gong I held in the middle

indicators.note: held means the medal word holds the I inside it

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal

explanation.surface: Someone holds a gong between their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gong' is British slang for a medal or decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Medial means situated at the centre, so placed in the middle.

clue.text: "This other Eden … " is partly spoken in defiance

indicators.note: partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Richard II praising England, quoted as if in defiance.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation comes from John of Gaunt's speech about England.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a retort that rubs in a point, as in a defiant 'so there!'

clue.text: Cheers, expression of dissent being banned

parts.note: ta and cheers are both British ways of saying thanks
boo is a jeer of disapproval

explanation.surface: A crowd mixes applause and jeers at something forbidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' means thanks, not applause.
explanation.definitionFit: A taboo subject is prohibited by custom, so it is forbidden.

clue.text: Doctor's back after unknown infection

indicators.note: after puts the back word behind the others

parts.note: Z is an algebraic unknown
HIV is a viral infection
ago means back in time, as in years back

explanation.surface: A doctor has returned after catching an unidentified bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' means in the past, not a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Zhivago is the title character of Pasternak's novel.

clue.text: Party in South Africa terminal for black priest

parts.note: ZA is the international code for South Africa
a do is a party

indicators.note: terminal means at the end, so the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A political party in South Africa stands at the end for black people.
explanation.definitionFit: Zadok was the high priest who anointed Solomon in the Bible.

clue.text: Interrogated with pants down?

parts.note: read as ..., having one's briefs (underpants) taken off, as well as being questioned after a mission

explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' is British for underpants, which are also called briefs.
explanation.definitionFit: After a mission an agent is questioned in detail, and the word also suggests having one's underwear removed.

clue.text: Became aware of a pan at back of stove

parts.note: a wok is a Chinese frying pan

indicators.note: at the back of means the final letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone notices a pan sitting at the back of the stove.
explanation.definitionFit: To wake up is to become conscious, so becoming aware.

clue.text: Prestige car is offered to woman and son? They go on foot

parts.note: Roller is slang for a Rolls-Royce
is shortens to 's
Kate is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A luxury car is given to a mother and her boy, who would otherwise walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They go on foot' suggests walkers, but means things worn on the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheeled boots are strapped to the feet, so they literally travel on foot.
